notes: It flies at night

blocks.prompt: Read this out loud
blocks.text: This is a moth. The moth flies at night. It has soft wings. It has fuzzy legs. All day long the moth rests. It sleeps on a tree. When the sun goes down, the moth wakes up. It flies to a white flower. It drinks the sweet nectar. Then it flies to the porch light. It goes around and around and around. In the morning the moth goes back to the tree. It closes its wings and sleeps.

blocks.prompt: How to Tell a Moth From a Butterfly
blocks.text: A butterfly flies when the sun is up. A moth flies when the sun goes down. That is one way to tell them apart. Here is another way. Look at the feelers on top of the head. A butterfly has two thin feelers with a little knob on the end. A moth has feelers shaped like tiny feathers or combs. A moth uses those feathery feelers to smell the night air. It can smell a flower long before it can see one. A moth is soft and fuzzy, as if it is wearing a coat. The fuzz keeps the moth warm, because at night there is no sun to warm it up.

answers: at night, when the sun goes down
like tiny feathers or combs
it keeps the moth warm

blocks.prompt: The Moth With No Mouth
blocks.text: Every moth starts as an egg smaller than a grain of sand. Out of the egg crawls a caterpillar, and a caterpillar has one job: eat. It chews leaves for weeks. It grows so fast that it splits its own skin and climbs out of it, sometimes four or five times. When it has eaten enough, it spins a cocoon out of silk that comes from its mouth. Inside that cocoon, the caterpillar takes its own body apart and builds a new one. Later, a moth pushes its way out. Its wings come out wet and crumpled. The moth pumps them full of fluid until they stretch flat and dry, and then it can fly. Some moths never eat again. The luna moth is a big pale green moth that lives in North America. When it comes out of its cocoon, it has no working mouth at all. It cannot feed. It lives about one week on the fat it stored back when it was a caterpillar. In that one week it has to find a mate and lay its eggs. That is the whole plan. All the eating happened first. All the flying happens now.

answers: to eat leaves and grow
from the caterpillar's mouth
it comes out of its cocoon with no working mouth
(inference: it only lives about a week, so there is no time to waste)

notes: Feathery antennae are chemical detectors
A pheromone is a scent signal
Many moths have ears that hear bat calls
Tiger moths click back at hunting bats
A luna moth's long tails confuse bat sonar
Moths are night pollinators

blocks.prompt: A Nose Like a Feather, and Ears for Bats
blocks.text: Look closely at a male silk moth and you will see two enormous feathery antennae fanning out from its head. They are not decoration and they are not for hearing. They are a nose, and it is one of the finest noses on Earth. A female silk moth releases a scent signal called a pheromone into the night air. The male's antennae are branched into thousands of tiny hairs, and each hair is dotted with pores. Air flows through the antenna like wind through a net, and the pores catch the drifting scent molecules. A male can pick up a female's signal from hundreds of yards away, in the dark, with no map. He simply turns toward wherever the scent is strongest and keeps flying. Scientists worked out the exact chemical for the silk moth in 1959, after grinding up half a million females to collect enough of it to study. The night is not a safe place, though. Bats hunt by shouting and listening for echoes, and moths are on the menu. So moths grew defenses. Many species have simple ears, sometimes on the chest, sometimes on the belly, tuned to the exact pitch of a hunting bat. When a moth hears the call, it folds its wings and drops out of the sky. Tiger moths go further. They answer the bat with rapid ultrasonic clicks of their own, which scramble the bat's echoes and make the moth hard to place. The luna moth uses a different trick entirely. Its two long trailing tails spin as it flies and throw back a false echo, so the bat strikes the tail and the moth flutters away with a torn ribbon and a whole body.

answers: (a scent signal an animal releases to send a message to another of its kind)
it is branched into thousands of hairs with pores, so air flows through and the pores catch scent molecules
he turns toward wherever the scent is strongest and keeps flying
(inference: a torn tail is survivable, being eaten is not)

notes: Roughly 160,000 known moth species

2024 cameras showed something different
Insects tilt their backs toward the brightest light
The sky is normally the brightest thing above
Artificial light traps moths in orbits

blocks.prompt: Why the Moth Cannot Leave the Light
blocks.text: Everyone has watched it happen. A moth arrives at a porch light and then cannot leave. It circles, climbs, stalls, drops, and circles again, for hours, until it is exhausted. For a hundred years the standard explanation was elegant and confident. Moths, the story went, navigate by the moon. Because the moon is impossibly far away, its light arrives in parallel lines, so a moth can hold a steady course simply by keeping the moon at a fixed angle to its body. This is called transverse orientation. A light bulb ruins the arithmetic. Its light radiates outward in all directions, so a moth holding a constant angle to a nearby bulb is not flying straight at all. It is tracing a spiral that tightens until it arrives at the glass. The explanation appeared in textbooks for decades. It had one weakness. Moths do not actually spiral inward. Watch carefully and you see something messier: orbiting, sudden climbs, stalls, and upside down tumbles. In 2024, a team of researchers finally settled it by filming flying insects around lights with high speed cameras and motion capture, the same technology used to animate films. What they found was almost the opposite of the old story. The insects were not steering toward the light. They were turning their backs to it. Flying animals need to know which way is up, and for hundreds of millions of years the answer has been reliable: up is where the sky glows. So insects evolved a simple rule called the dorsal light response, meaning they tilt their upper side toward the brightest region and let that keep them level. Under an open sky the rule works perfectly. Under a porch light it becomes a trap. The moth banks so its back faces the bulb, which tips it into an endless orbit around it. Fly above the light and the moth flips over. Fly beneath it and the moth stalls and falls. The moth is not drawn to the light. It is being lied to about which way is up, and it cannot argue with the sky. That correction matters beyond curiosity. Moths are major pollinators of night blooming plants, and their numbers are falling across much of the world. Every bright bulb left on all night is a small machine for removing them from the dark places where they do their work.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Biston betularia, the peppered moth
Pale speckled form: typica
Soot black form: carbonaria
First black one recorded in Manchester, 1848
Around 98 percent black by 1895
The mutation was traced to a jumping gene in 2016

blocks.prompt: The Moth That Changed Color in Fifty Years
blocks.text: The peppered moth is a plain animal with an extraordinary record. For as long as English naturalists had been collecting insects, it came in one pattern: white speckled with fine black flecks, a scatter of pepper on a pale wing. Resting on a lichen crusted tree trunk it more or less disappeared. Collectors called this form typica, and nobody wrote much about it, because there was nothing to write. Then, in 1848, a collector in Manchester recorded a peppered moth that was entirely black. It was a curiosity, a one off, worth a note in a journal. By 1895, roughly 98 percent of the peppered moths in Manchester were black. Something had happened, and it had happened faster than anyone thought living things could change. What happened was coal. Manchester was the furnace of the industrial revolution, and the smoke pouring out of it did two things to the surrounding woods. Soot blackened the bark, and sulfur dioxide killed the pale lichens growing on it. In fifty years the moth's living room had been repainted. On a clean lichened trunk, the speckled typica was invisible and a black moth was an obvious target. On a bare sooty trunk, the arrangement reversed. Birds, hunting by sight, did the rest. They ate whichever moths they could see, and every moth they missed passed its pattern to the next generation. The black form, carbonaria, had gone from a single specimen to a near monopoly in about forty moth generations, not because any moth changed color, but because the birds kept editing the population. Bernard Kettlewell tested this in the 1950s by releasing marked moths in polluted and unpolluted woods and recapturing what survived. His results matched the story, and the peppered moth marched into every biology textbook in the world. Then critics found real problems with his methods: he released moths in daylight, in unnatural numbers, and sometimes pinned them where they would never naturally rest. For a while the most famous example of evolution in action was also one of the most disputed. Science answered the way it should. Michael Majerus spent seven years running the experiment again, more carefully, with moths in natural resting positions and predation watched directly. He died before publishing. His colleagues published the results in 2012, and the results were unambiguous: birds ate the conspicuous moths, and that alone accounted for the change. Then the story got better. In 2016, geneticists located the exact mutation behind carbonaria. It was a transposable element, a stretch of DNA that copies itself and jumps into new positions, which had landed inside a gene called cortex. They estimated it arrived around 1819, which fits a first sighting in 1848 almost perfectly. And there is a final chapter that most textbooks skip. Britain passed clean air laws in the 1950s and 1960s. The soot thinned, the lichens crept back, the trunks turned pale again, and the black moths began to vanish. Today carbonaria is rare once more. The experiment ran forward and then ran backward, and the moth followed the trunks both times, without ever knowing it was the evidence.

(individuals never changed; birds removed the visible ones and survivors passed on their pattern; cite: not because any moth changed color, but because the birds kept editing the population)
(soot blackened bark and sulfur dioxide killed the pale lichens, so the pale form became conspicuous and the black form hid)
(he released moths in daylight, in unnatural numbers, and pinned them in unnatural positions; Majerus repeated it properly and the 2012 results confirmed bird predation)
(the moth was evidence of natural selection without any awareness of it; supported by the forward and backward runs of the change)
